messages.author: 13d0e40ead8b0219
messages.subject: GIGAMUGA mapping issues
parts:
Hello,

I followed the guide for preparing DO mouse data for qtl2 for my GIGAMUGA data (http://kbroman.org/qtl2/pages/prep_do_data.html), but I've been getting strange issues after mapping.

Upon calculating QTL effects with scan1coef(), I've noticed that certain chromosomes return very strange results (refer to chrom1.png), while other chromosomes return more typical-looking results (chrom2.png)

When I looked at the range of values for the 6th allele in my scan1coef() object for chromosome 1, I noted the following strange results:

> range(na.omit(coef_c2[,6]))
[1] -172696229324     249156537

while the "real" range is the following:

> range(na.omit(coef_c2[,5]))
[1] 1.592147 4.778550

This error seems to occur in chromosomes 2,5,6,8,11,13,14,15,16,18 and X, and as far as I can tell, is not restricted to the 6th allele.

Any help would be appreciated.

-Basel Al-Barghouthi

parts:
A problem with this graph is it highlights any artifacts.

At a locus where one of the 8 alleles is absent, the estimated effect for that allele can't be estimated. But rather than returning missing values, scan1coef() is giving crazy large values (though with corresponding crazy large SEs).

karl

messages.author: 13d0e40ead8b0219
messages.subject: Re: GIGAMUGA mapping issues
parts:
What would cause this phenomenon to be spread across chromsomes, but not traits?
For example, a trait for which there are only 56 data points shows a "normal" graph on chrom 1, but the trait with 192 data points could be affected greatly by these artifacts on chromosome 2.

-Basel

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: GIGAMUGA mapping issues
parts:
On chr 2, there's a position where H is not present in any of the 192 mice.
On other chromosomes, all alleles are present in the full 192 mice, but when you reduce to 56 mice, there'll be alleles missing from those 56 at particular positions.

karl

In the short term, you might replace the extreme values with NA.
Something like this, I think:

co[abs(co) > diff(range(x$pheno[,65],na.rm=TRUE))] <- NA

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] GIGAMUGA mapping issues
parts:
Perhaps to illustrate further, if I take the sum of the allele probs at a certain marker for all 8 alleles, i don't get the expected 12.5% across all 8 alleles (for example, sum(apr$`2`[,6,"UNCHS004230"]) returns 7. Given 192 samples, 7/384 alleles give a prob of 1.82%)

I created a matrix of the sum of allele probabilities for all 8 alleles across all markers, and counted the number of markers that show a sum(apr) of less than 10 for any of the 8 alleles (about 2.6% allele frequency)

I got the following number of markers per chromosome that met this criteria:

   1      13   14   15    16     17   18    2     20    5
8701  145   71  166  170   52    3  485  131   42

Doesn't this indicate that something is wrong? Incidentally, those chromosomes all had strange coef_CC plots, with the exception of chrom 1.

I don't understand what it is you're plotting. Can you provide more detailed code?

> Perhaps to illustrate further, if I take the sum of the allele probs at a certain marker for all 8 alleles, i don't get the expected 12.5% across all 8 alleles (for example, sum(apr$`2`[,6,"UNCHS004230"]) returns 7. Given 192 samples, 7/384 alleles give a prob of 1.82%)
>
> I created a matrix of the sum of allele probabilities for all 8 alleles across all markers, and counted the number of markers that show a sum(apr) of less than 10 for any of the 8 alleles (about 2.6% allele frequency)
>
> I got the following number of markers per chromosome that met this criteria:

> 1 13 14 15 16 17 18 2 20 5
> 8701 145 71 166 170 52 3 485 131 42
>
> Doesn't this indicate that something is wrong? Incidentally, those chromosomes all had strange coef_CC plots, with the exception of chrom 1.

I wasn't able to find anything obviously wrong with the data. With 192 mice, it shouldn't be a surprise to find some regions with missing alleles. And when you reduce to ~60 mice for some phenotypes, there will be loads of such places.

And you can potentially obtain good evidence for genotype:phenotype association even if some of the possible genotypes were not observed.

karl

parts:
The first 8 coefficients are the allele effects, and they should be like phenotype averages, and so within the range of the phenotype distribution. So in removing the excessive values, do the following (rather than what I'd written):

r <- range(cross$pheno[,58], na.rm=TRUE)
for(i in 1:8)
coef_c2[ coef_c2[,i] < r[1] | coef_c2[,i] > r[2], i] <- NA

karl
